strengths: Novel identification and empirical validation of the sparsity paradox in sparse-attention training, where Sparse-Sparse models unexpectedly exhibit lower attention sparsity than Full-Full models
Clear problem diagnosis (gradient update deficiency) with intuitive solution combining dual-stream training and bidirectional alignment loss that maintains gradient flow to all tokens

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: perplexity, commonsense reasoning (4 benchmarks), long-context understanding (LongBench, NIAH, PG19), and extrapolation with rigorous ablations

Valuable mechanistic insights including connection between sparse-attention training and improved length extrapolation, with detailed analysis of attention sink phenomenon and visualizations across context lengths
Consistent improvements across sparse-inference tasks with strong performance on LongBench (20.75% vs NSA 18.21% at 1024 receptive field)
Clear presentation with well-motivated Figure 1, detailed Algorithm 1, comprehensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Root cause hypothesis (gradient update deficiency) is intuitive but unvalidated—lacks direct evidence such as gradient magnitude distributions across ranked key-value pairs to confirm the diagnosis
Alignment loss design choices not justified: why SmoothL1 over alternatives (L2, KL divergence)? Limited ablation on loss function choices despite this being central to the method
Training efficiency claims lack quantitative support—no timing comparisons, FLOPs analysis, or memory overhead despite computing both full and sparse attention for auxiliary objectives

Attention sparsity metric (Eq. 6) is somewhat circular: measuring attention mass in pre-selected top-k blocks reflects selection quality rather than inherent model sparsity, potentially explaining observed differences

Marginal full-attention gains undermine a key motivation: Table 1 shows 60.22% vs FullAttn 59.48% on benchmarks (0.74%) and 15.19 vs 15.18 PPL (negligible), while sparse-inference improvements are stronger
Confounding experimental factors: gated attention applied to all baselines has substantial impact (Table 5: 0.67% improvement), reducing confidence in fair comparison; reduced KV-heads not isolated
Technical novelty is moderate—combines existing ideas (dual-stream training, knowledge distillation, VQ-VAE commitment loss) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts
Limited to 1B parameter models; larger-scale evaluation (7B+) would be more compelling for ICML 2026, especially given rapid LLM development
Receptive field handling unclear: reporting SSA-16×16 'extrapolated' to 1024 lacks clarity on methodology; Table 8 shows marginal differences (SSA 15.39 vs NSA 15.48 at 32×32)

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Table 3 shows significant α dependence and receptive-field 'sweet spot' requirement, but limited guidance on selection; 50/50 sampling ratio lacks justification
Important details relegated to appendices: gated attention's impact (Table 5) should be in main text given significance for baseline fairness

Missing comparisons with recent methods (DSA, InfLLM-v2 briefly mentioned but not evaluated); claim about 'smooth adaptation to varying sparsity' is misleading (only varies at inference, not training)

strengths: Identifies an interesting and counterintuitive paradox: sparse-attention-trained models exhibit lower attention sparsity than full-attention models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and long-context understanding with detailed ablations
Insightful analysis of attention sink phenomenon and its relationship to training methodology and length extrapolation
Clear presentation with well-designed visualizations (especially attention distribution analyses) and reproducibility details documented
Proposes a simple and implementable solution that achieves improvements across multiple benchmarks
weaknesses: Core causal mechanism unvalidated: claims gradient deficiency causes low sparsity but doesn't prove the alignment solution addresses this root cause; mechanism could simply be regularization-based

Critical experimental concern: SSA-1024 results obtained by 'extrapolating' 256-receptive-field model rather than training directly; Table 3 shows training with larger receptive fields degrades performance, suggesting alignment loss acts as unintended regularization
Limited scale: main experiments on 1B models trained on 100B tokens (small for 2026); no experiments on 7B+ models; generalizability to production-scale models unclear
Modest performance improvements: often 1-2% gains (e.g., commonsense 60.22% vs 59.48%); unclear if these justify added complexity and hyperparameter tuning
High hyperparameter sensitivity: Table 3 ablations show training failures (NaN) with certain configurations; requires careful tuning of α, FullRatio, and receptive field; suggests method is fragile
Incomplete ablations on core mechanism: cannot isolate which component (dual streaming vs. alignment loss) drives improvements; several ablations fail to train
Gated attention confound: all baselines use gated attention which significantly impacts results (Appendix B); makes isolating SSA's true contribution difficult
Insufficient baseline comparisons: missing recent methods (InfLLM-v2, DSA mentioned but not compared); only compared to MoBA and NSA

Attention sparsity metric circularity: metric directly measures concentration in top-k blocks; training with sparsity-encouraging alignment loss trivially improves this metric without validating gradient hypothesis
Limited novelty: bidirectional alignment is straightforward application of knowledge distillation/commitment loss ideas (all properly cited); primarily engineering contribution
Efficiency claims unsupported: states training cost 'marginally increased' without quantification; no wall-clock comparisons or FLOPs analysis
Missing mechanistic understanding: does not explain why alignment specifically improves extrapolation, why certain hyperparameters work, or how streams interact during optimization

strengths: Novel empirical observation: The paradox that sparse-attention-trained models exhibit lower inherent attention sparsity than full-attention models is well-documented (Figure 1d) and counterintuitive, providing valuable insight for the sparse attention community

Sound and practical methodology: The dual-stream training approach with bidirectional alignment is well-motivated, with Algorithm 1 providing clear, implementable pseudocode. The alternating optimization maintains fair computation with baselines.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive benchmarks across commonsense reasoning, language modeling, and long-context understanding (NIAH, LongBench, perplexity). Consistent improvements across both sparse and full-attention inference modes.
Strong empirical ablations: Table 3 systematically validates each component's contribution. The paper clearly demonstrates that bidirectional alignment and dual-stream training are necessary.
Practical value and flexibility: SSA enables smooth extrapolation across sparsity levels (Figure 3) and improves single-model performance under both inference modes—valuable for deployment scenarios.

Mechanistic insights: The connection between sparse attention training and mitigation of attention sinks (Section 5.4, Figures 6-12) provides valuable understanding beyond the core contribution, with detailed visualizations supporting the analysis.
Clear presentation: Well-structured motivation, precise mathematical formulation, thorough implementation details in appendices, and effective use of visualizations in main paper.
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical justification: While the 'gradient update deficiency' explanation is intuitive, it lacks direct empirical support. The paper provides no gradient flow analysis showing excluded KV pairs receive zero gradients, no visualization of attention weight evolution during training, and no ablation isolating gradient preservation from alignment loss effects.

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: (1) All baselines use gated attention—authors acknowledge this partly explains NSA's gains but don't fully quantify its isolated contribution; (2) Receptive field 1024 results are obtained by 'extrapolating' 256-model performance rather than direct training; (3) NSA has 1.5× larger receptive field due to sliding-window; (4) num_head_kv reduced to 2, potentially disadvantaging some baselines.

Training cost not quantified: Claims training overhead is 'marginal' but provides no concrete number (percentage increase). No memory overhead analysis provided, which is crucial for practitioner adoption decisions.

Marginal improvements on some benchmarks: Commonsense reasoning gains are often <1% over FullAttn (Table 1). No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported, making it unclear if differences are meaningful.
Limited experimental scale: Only tested up to 1B parameters—unclear if improvements persist at 7B, 13B, 70B scales. Single architecture family (Llama-3.2). Single pretraining corpus (SmolLM).

Incomplete failure analysis: Table 3 shows unidirectional alignment and random layer assignment catastrophically fail (NaN). The paper provides no analysis of why or what causes the instability, limiting understanding of the bidirectional alignment necessity.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Multiple sensitive parameters (α, FullRatio, receptive field). Table 3 shows nontrivial sensitivity to all three. Limited practical guidance on setting these for different applications.

Insufficient analysis of attention alignment alternatives: The paper doesn't thoroughly justify why L1 alignment (SmoothL1) is optimal vs. L2 or KL divergence. Brief mention of avoiding dense attention materialization, but no empirical timing comparison.
Unclear mechanisms of benefit: The paper doesn't clearly identify which characteristics (attention sink mitigation vs. sparsity regularization vs. other factors) drive improvements in which tasks.
Missing comparisons: Limited to MoBA and NSA comparisons. Other sparse variants (InfLLM-v2, DSA) mentioned but not experimentally compared.

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying and formalizing two complementary deficiencies in sparse attention (attention gap and capability gap) with well-motivated theoretical decomposition

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions (perplexity, commonsense reasoning, long-context tasks) with systematic ablations, multiple seeds, and detailed reproducibility information
Strong and consistent improvements across both full and sparse inference modes, demonstrating genuine compatibility rather than trade-offs
Theoretically motivated design with Theorem 1 providing approximation error bounds and direct connection to alignment objectives
Practical efficiency gains (17% training overhead, 2× speedup at 128k) with demonstrated superior extrapolation to varying sparsity levels
Honest treatment of limitations including out-of-distribution performance degradation (NIAH >8k) and training instability without alignment
weaknesses: Limited model scale (only 1B and 300M parameters) with no experiments on 7B/13B+ models, raising concerns about production applicability and generalization of findings

Experimental fairness issues: SSA trained at RF=256 but results reported for RF=1024 by extrapolation while baselines are trained at target configurations; NSA excluded from full-attention evaluation; all methods use reduced KV heads incompatible with full-attention optimization

Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 1 is a straightforward application of triangle inequality with potentially loose bounds; Propositions 4.1-4.2 capture well-known observations about gradient flow and distribution mismatch rather than novel insights

Alignment mechanism fails on out-of-distribution contexts (NIAH performance collapses beyond 8k), contradicting long-context goals and suggesting position-agnostic methods (like MoBA) may be preferable
Insufficient justification for design choices: asymmetric stop-gradients in alignment loss, no systematic exploration of alternatives, fragile training (NaN with random/one-directional alignment)

Unexplained 'sweet spot' phenomenon (Section 7.5) where smaller receptive fields outperform larger ones, suggesting potential overfitting to alignment signal and limiting hyperparameter guidance for new settings
Statistical concerns: some improvements within standard deviation ranges (Table 1); LongBench and NIAH on single runs only; no significance testing provided
Incomplete analysis: limited visualization of learned attention patterns, insufficient exploration of when/why SSA outperforms baselines, missing investigations of downstream fine-tuning

strengths: Clear articulation of the two gaps (attention gap and capability gap) in sparse attention training
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across perplexity, commonsense reasoning, and long-context tasks with both inference modes
Consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks with reasonable ablation studies
Well-organized presentation with clear figures and extensive implementation details in appendices
Achieves higher attention sparsity than baselines (Figure 1d)
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions are limited: Propositions 4.1-4.2 formalize obvious facts rather than provide deep insights; Theorem 1 provides a loose bound with no analysis of tightness or practical validation

Method novelty is limited: dual-stream training + bidirectional alignment losses are straightforward combinations of existing techniques (VQ-VAE, RLHF); core idea is essentially knowledge distillation without being positioned as such

Critical experimental concern: receptive field 'extrapolation' from 256 to 1024 is poorly explained and suspicious—it's unclear if models are trained separately or if results involve true extrapolation, undermining the main experimental narrative
Severely limited scale: evaluation restricted to 1B and 300M models with no evidence of scalability to modern LLMs (7B-70B); unclear if modest improvements generalize to larger models

Long-context generalization failure: Table 3 shows significant NIAH performance degradation beyond 8k tokens (the training context), contradicting core sparse attention motivation for long contexts; paper acknowledges but provides no solution
Modest improvements with overlapping error bars: many gains are 0.3-1% and fall within confidence intervals (e.g., Table 1: 74.54±0.48 vs 74.17±0.37); unclear if statistically significant
Incomplete baseline comparisons: NSA excluded from full-attention evaluation; NSA's sliding window component is crucial to performance (Appendix G), confounding sparse design with other mechanisms

Missing mechanistic analysis: why does alignment loss produce NaN when applied uni-directionally (Table 2)? What explains the dramatic NIAH degradation beyond 8k? Why does higher sparsity not always help (Section 7.5)?
Insufficient justification for design choices: 50-50 alternation ratio not ablated; value-level alignment chosen for efficiency, not principled reasons; alignment weight α requires tuning (Table A14)
Limited generalization: single domain (language modeling), single language (English), no evidence of domain transfer or multilingual applicability

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework identifying and formalizing attention gap (Prop 4.2) and capability gap (Prop 4.1) with Theorem 1 providing interpretable error bounds
Elegant and practical solution: dual-stream training with bidirectional alignment is simple yet effective, with reasonable 17% training overhead
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple dimensions: perplexity, commonsense reasoning, long-context understanding (LongBench, NIAH, PG-19) with 5 runs and fixed seeds
Consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks and sparsity levels (RF 256-4096); strong extrapolation properties demonstrated in Figure 3
Novel insight into RoPE frequency aliasing and explanation of sparse attention's robustness to length extrapolation (Appendix L)
Flexibility to work in both sparse and full inference modes without retraining; adapts to varying sparsity budgets
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, code to be released, transparent reporting with honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Theoretical bound (Theorem 1) may be loose, depending on unknown quantities; no empirical validation that the bound predicts actual performance or guides optimization; missing explicit connection between alignment loss and minimizing δ(t)
Limited to small models (1B, 300M); unclear if improvements scale to 7B+ models critical for practical deployment

Generalization beyond training distribution is limited: NIAH performance drops sharply beyond 8k context (70.6% at 16k vs 92.6% at 8k), undermining 'superior long-context' claims; authors acknowledge this limitation but don't adequately address it

Experimental fairness concerns: SSA's RF=1024 results are obtained by extrapolating the RF=256 model rather than training with RF=1024, unlike baselines; this gives SSA an algorithmic advantage that isn't immediately apparent

Modest empirical improvements on many core tasks: ~1-2% on commonsense reasoning and perplexity, sometimes within error margins; while consistent, gains may not justify added complexity for practitioners

Design choices lack strong justification: equal streaming probability (50-50) not ablated; SmoothL1 vs L2 shows minimal difference; α=10 chosen without sensitivity analysis; Table 2 shows NaN for unidirectional alignment without explanation

Incomplete analysis of why sparser attention benefits downstream reasoning (Section 7.2) and why SSA outperforms FullAttn on benchmarks despite higher PPL (Section 7.1); these warrant deeper investigation
Missing critical experiments: no scaling to larger models, no ablation on stream probability, limited analysis of when/why SSA fails (e.g., NIAH > 8k)
